1: # Gatekeeper ZoomInfo
2: 
3: This package provides [ZoomInfo](https://www.zoominfo.com) integration for Gadgets via ZoomInfo's
4: GTM (go-to-market) API, using OAuth2 (Authorization Code + PKCE).
5: 
6: It exposes a single **whole-account** resource (`https://app.zoominfo.com/`): a session scoped to one
7: connected ZoomInfo account's OAuth grant and package entitlements. Through it a gadget can:
8: 
9: - **Lookup** — resolve controlled filter values (industries, intent topics, scoop types, …) and
10:   discover the enrich fields the account is entitled to.
11: - **Search** (free) — companies, contacts, intent signals, scoops, and news, with full firmographic
12:   and technographic filter fidelity.
13: - **Enrich** (consumes credits) — turn matched records into full detail: companies, contacts,
14:   corporate hierarchy, hashtags, intent, scoops, and news.
15: - **Copilot** — company/contact lookalikes, contact recommendations, AI account summaries (+ ask),
16:   and curated company insight signals.
17: - **Usage** — read the account's credit/limit counters.
18: 
19: A connected account corresponds to the ZoomInfo user who authorizes the OAuth consent flow. ZoomInfo
20: is **not** offered as a "Continue with…" sign-in method (`getAuthenticatedEmail()` returns `null`).
21: 
22: ## Creating the OAuth app
23: 
24: 1. In the [ZoomInfo Developer Portal](https://api.zoominfo.com/), create an OAuth application.
25: 2. Set the **Redirect URI** to your deployment's callback (replace the host with your base URL):
26: 
27:    ```
28:    ${BASE_URL}/gatekeeper/zoominfo/oauth
29:    ```
30: 
31:    For local development that is `http://localhost:8787/gatekeeper/zoominfo/oauth`.
32: 3. Enable all API scopes the account is entitled to. The gatekeeper requests exactly the scopes
33:    ZoomInfo's authorization server recognizes:
34: 
35:    ```
36:    api:data:company  api:data:contact  api:data:intent  api:data:news  api:data:scoops
37:    api:recommendations:read  api:account-summary:read  api:insights:read
38:    ```
39: 
40:    There is no `lookup` scope — lookup/enrich-field reference data comes with the data scopes.
41: 4. Copy the **Client ID** and **Client Secret**.
42: 
43: > Use the OAuth app's **Client ID + Client Secret**. The `authorization_code` exchange posts them to
44: > the token endpoint as HTTP Basic auth (form-urlencoded), with PKCE (S256) and refresh-token
45: > rotation.
46: 
47: ## Configuration
48: 
49: The gatekeeper Worker reads `CLIENT_ID` and `CLIENT_SECRET`. In local development these are seeded
50: from the root `.dev.vars` by `run-dev-server.ts`:
51: 
52: ```
53: ZOOMINFO_CLIENT_ID=<oauth app client id>
54: ZOOMINFO_CLIENT_SECRET=<oauth app client secret>
55: ```
56: 
57: Optional overrides read by the Worker:
58: 
59: - `BASE_URL` — the gatekeeper's public base (default `http://localhost:8787/gatekeeper/zoominfo`);
60:   the OAuth redirect is `${BASE_URL}/oauth`.
61: - `ZOOMINFO_API_BASE_URL` — the ZoomInfo API root (default `https://api.zoominfo.com/gtm`).
62: 
63: ## Notes & limitations
64: 
65: - **Credits.** Search, lookup, recommendations, insights, and account summaries are free. Enrichment
66:   consumes ZoomInfo credits (roughly one per newly-enriched record; already-owned records and
67:   no-match/error results are free). `getCreditUsage()` is the authoritative source for accounting —
68:   the per-record `creditCharged` flag is a display-only upper bound, because ZoomInfo often omits
69:   management status from enrich responses and so over-reports records served for free.
70: - **Approvals.** Reads are logged as observations. Each `enrich*` call is submitted to the approval
71:   queue and spends credits only once a human approves it; results are fetched afterward via
72:   `getEnrichmentResult(ticket)`. Enrichments are **not** simulated — the action carries
73:   `awaitDecision`, so the agent turn suspends until the decision rather than reading back
74:   un-enriched state.
75: - **Intent/scoop company targeting.** Intent and scoop *search* filter by firmographics only —
76:   ZoomInfo has no company-identity inputs there. To pull intent or scoops for a specific known
77:   company, use `enrichIntent` / `enrichScoops` (which take a company identifier). The API surface and
78:   a runtime guard both enforce this with a clear message instead of ZoomInfo's opaque 400.
79: - **`state` vs `country`.** These are mutually exclusive: ZoomInfo silently ignores `state` when
80:   `country` is also set and returns the whole country. The gatekeeper rejects the combination up
81:   front rather than returning broadened results with no signal. `state` already scopes to the
82:   US/Canada, so pass just one.
83: - **Entitlements.** Every call is scoped to the account's package: ZoomInfo returns only the fields
84:   and datasets the account is entitled to; unentitled fields come back empty.
85: 
86: ## Troubleshooting
87: 
88: ### "ZoomInfo Gatekeeper Not Configured" during authorization
89: 
90: `CLIENT_ID` or `CLIENT_SECRET` is missing. Ensure `ZOOMINFO_CLIENT_ID` / `ZOOMINFO_CLIENT_SECRET`
91: are set in the root `.dev.vars`, then restart the dev server.
92: 
93: ### `invalid_scope` on the authorization page
94: 
95: A requested scope isn't recognized by ZoomInfo's authorization server. Confirm the app has the eight
96: scopes listed above enabled and that no others are being requested.
97: 
98: ### Redirect URI mismatch
99: 
100: The redirect URI sent must exactly match one registered on the app. Confirm the portal has
101: `${BASE_URL}/gatekeeper/zoominfo/oauth` (for local dev,
102: `http://localhost:8787/gatekeeper/zoominfo/oauth`, no trailing slash).
103: 
104: ### "ZoomInfo did not return a refresh token"
105: 
106: The OAuth app isn't issuing refresh tokens. Enable the refresh-token grant for the app in the
107: Developer Portal and reconnect — the gatekeeper needs a refresh token to keep the long-lived session
108: alive after the access token expires.

(End of file - total 108 lines)
</content>

   ```

   There is no `lookup` scope — lookup/enrich-field reference data comes with the data scopes.
4. Copy the **Client ID** and **Client Secret**.

> rotation.

  queue and spends credits only once a human approves it; results are fetched afterward via

  un-enriched state.
- **Intent/scoop company targeting.** Intent and scoop *search* filter by firmographics only —

display.text:
# Gatekeeper Supabase

This package provides Supabase integration for Gadgets via the [Supabase Management
API](https://supabase.com/docs/reference/api/introduction), using OAuth2.

It exposes two resource granularities:

- **Project** (`https://supabase.com/dashboard/project/:ref`) — the recommended unit. A project is a
  hosted Postgres database plus its auth, storage, and edge functions. Gadgets can run read-only and
  (approval-gated) mutating SQL, introspect schema, and list edge functions and storage buckets.
- **Organization** (`https://supabase.com/dashboard/org/:slug`) — broader access to discover and act
  across every project in an organization.

A connected account corresponds to the organization the user authorizes during the OAuth consent
flow.

## Creating the OAuth app

1. In your Supabase **organization settings**, open the **OAuth Apps** tab
   (`https://supabase.com/dashboard/org/_/apps`) and **Add application**.
2. Set the **Redirect URI** to your deployment's callback (replace the host with `PUBLIC_BASE_URL`):

   ```
   ${PUBLIC_BASE_URL}/gatekeeper/supabase/oauth
   ```

   For local development that is `http://localhost:8787/gatekeeper/supabase/oauth`.
3. After creating it, copy the **Client ID** and **Client Secret** (the secret is shown once).

> Use the OAuth app's **Client ID + Client Secret** — not a personal access token or project API
> key. The `authorization_code` exchange requires the OAuth app credentials.

## Configuration

The gatekeeper Worker reads `CLIENT_ID` and `CLIENT_SECRET`. In local development these are seeded
from shell/`.dev.vars` variables by `run-dev-server.ts`:

```
SUPABASE_CLIENT_ID=<oauth app client id>
SUPABASE_CLIENT_SECRET=<oauth app client secret>
```

## Notes

- Reads are logged as observations; mutating SQL (`execute()`) is submitted to the approval queue
  and only runs once a human approves it.
- Mutating SQL is **not** simulated — arbitrary statements cannot be reliably previewed through the
  stateless query endpoint, so a `query()` will not observe an un-approved change. This is
  documented in the API types.

1: # Gatekeeper Cloudflare
2: 
3: This package provides Cloudflare OAuth integration for Gadgets. It serves three purposes:
4: 
5: - **Sign-in:** when `cloudflare` is in the deployment's `AUTH_GATEKEEPERS` allowlist, "Continue with
6:   Cloudflare" appears on the login page. The grant reads the account email (verified by Cloudflare,
7:   via the `/user` API), which becomes the user's identity. Cloudflare sign-in also establishes the
8:   persistent billing-only connection described below.
9: - **AI Gateway billing:** when a user connects Cloudflare or signs in with it, the billing scopes are
10:   requested and the connection persists. The Workshop then reads a usable access
11:   token from it (`getUsableAccessToken`) to power the [AI Gateway billing](../../docs/ai-gateway-billing.md)
12:   flow — reading the credit balance and routing BYOK inference through the account's default AI
13:   Gateway.
14: - **Workers Observability:** gadgets can receive read-only access to logs, events, invocations,
15:   aggregate metrics, and traces either across an account or restricted to one Worker. Every result
16:   is authorized as an observation, and Worker bindings inject an immutable service filter and
17:   defensively discard foreign-service events. Distributed trace summaries are account-only because
18:   their names, timing, services, and counts describe the whole cross-service trace; a Worker binding
19:   can still retrieve its own events for a known trace ID.
20: 
21: Observability connections request `workers-observability.read`. The OAuth client must allow that
22: scope or Cloudflare will omit/reject it. Existing billing-only connections can add the grant when the
23: user first selects an observability resource. Cloudflare exposes account and Worker resource choices,
24: but both map to this one indivisible OAuth scope; resource bindings provide the finer capability
25: boundary after connection.
26: 
27: Workers telemetry is retained by Cloudflare for at most seven days. Queries default to the last hour,
28: and the Worker picker searches the full retention window. Suggested bindings are
29: `CLOUDFLARE_OBSERVABILITY` for account access and `WORKER_OBSERVABILITY` for one Worker.
30: 
31: ### Sharing a gadget that reads telemetry
32: 
33: A binding is not transferable. When a gadget with an observability binding is shared, each
34: collaborator is admitted only if **their own** connected Cloudflare account can read that resource
35: (`addObserver` checks it against their credentials, not the owner's). A collaborator without access is
36: refused, and a verification that fails for any other reason — a 5xx, a transport error — is also a
37: refusal rather than an admission.
38: 
39: ### What a Worker binding trusts, and what it re-checks
40: 
41: The scope filter is prepended to every query, but a filter the provider *accepted* is not evidence it
42: *applied* it — three separate behaviours here return wrong-but-plausible data with no error. So events
43: are re-filtered on the way out, and a single foreign event is treated as proof the filter was dropped:
44: the provider's `count` is withheld (it would be a count of the whole account's matching telemetry) and
45: the event is logged at `error`. `statistics` is kept, because it describes what our query cost rather
46: than how much matched, and callers are told to read it for cost.
47: 
48: The re-check is deliberately not a hard failure. The events returned are filtered and therefore safe,
49: and this provider has surprised us often enough that turning a hypothetical disclosure into a
50: guaranteed outage would be the worse trade.
51: 
52: `calculate()` is the exception, and knowingly so: an aggregate cannot be un-mixed, so there is no
53: second line of defence to add. It rests entirely on the injected filter. The fix that would work —
54: grouping by `$metadata.service` and keeping this binding's own group, whose value *is* the correctly
55: scoped answer even for a median — changes `limit` and `orderBy` semantics for every caller, so it is a
56: follow-up rather than a footnote.
57: 
58: ### Why discovery sometimes costs a query
59: 
60: Cloudflare's `telemetry/keys` and `telemetry/values` endpoints ignore the `filters` array they accept:
61: verified against a live account, they answer for the whole account no matter what is passed. A
62: Worker-scoped binding therefore cannot use them — they would disclose every field name and value in
63: the account. Whenever a discovery call has to be constrained (a Worker binding, or any caller-supplied
64: filter), the answer is derived instead from a filtered `telemetry/query` events sample, which the
65: provider does filter correctly. Unconstrained account-wide discovery still uses the cheap endpoints.
66: 
67: > Unresolved: whether the `workers-observability.read` scope alone is accepted, or whether Cloudflare
68: > requires the Workers Observability **Write** permission to read telemetry. This has not been
69: > verified against a live token; if reads 403 on a correctly-scoped grant, that is the first thing to
70: > check.
71: 
72: ### Two names for one field
73: 
74: A log's own structured fields are returned nested under `source` but are **indexed under their bare
75: name**: `logger.warn(msg, {event: "x"})` comes back as `source.event` and is queried as `event`.
76: Confirmed both ways — `telemetry/keys` on a live account reports `event`/`component`/`level` and no
77: `source.*` key at all, and the [Workers Logs
78: docs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/observability/logs/workers-logs/) show
79: `console.log({user_id: 123})` being filtered as `user_id`.
80: 
81: This matters because the provider accepts an unknown filter key, matches nothing, and returns an empty
82: page with no error. So discovery reports indexed names (`observability-discovery.ts`), and
83: `observabilityFieldKey` additionally accepts a `source.`-prefixed key as an alias wherever a caller
84: names a field — filters, `calculations`, `groupBys`, `listValues` — because copying a path out of a
85: `listEvents` result is the obvious thing to do and used to fail silently.
86: 
87: `openid` is intentionally **not** requested — the Cloudflare dashboard OAuth client isn't permitted
88: that scope; identity comes from the `/user` API (`user-details.read`).
89: 
90: ### Why an error's text never reaches the log
91: 
92: `summarizeFilter` deliberately keeps filter *values* out of the audit trail — they are caller text.
93: But a provider error message can quote that same value straight back, so logging the message would
94: readmit through the error path exactly what the audit path excludes. `CloudflareObservabilityApiError`
95: therefore carries Cloudflare's numeric `codes` alongside the message: the request log names the
96: codes, and the message travels only to the caller who caused it.
97: 
98: The codes are not the discriminator, though — Cloudflare can return a message with no numeric code
99: at all, so the error records separately whether the message is *its* or *ours*, and only ours is
100: logged. A provider failure carrying no codes is therefore logged as a bare status, which is the
101: fail-closed answer: the status still says what happened without quoting anyone's filter back.
102: 
103: ### Listing accounts is a walk, not a request
104: 
105: `/accounts` is paginated and defaults to **20** per page, so a single GET silently returns a truncated
106: list — an account past the first page simply cannot be picked, with nothing to indicate why. The
107: account picker's substring match also stays client-side: `name` is the only documented server-side
108: filter and whether it matches exactly or by substring is not specified, so pushing it down would trade
109: a visible truncation for an invisible one.
110: 
111: ## Setting Up Cloudflare OAuth Credentials
112: 
113: You need a Cloudflare dashboard OAuth client (client id + secret). The dashboard OAuth endpoints and
114: scopes are hardcoded in `src/oauth.ts`, so you only configure the client id/secret and register the
115: redirect URI. Ensure the client's scope allowlist includes `workers-observability.read` when this
116: deployment offers Workers Observability resources.
117: 
118: ### Step 1: Register the redirect URI
119: 
120: The gatekeeper's OAuth redirect URI is:
121: 
122: ```
123: ${BASE_URL}/oauth
124: ```
125: 
126: where `BASE_URL` defaults to `http://localhost:8787/gatekeeper/cloudflare` in dev — i.e. the full
127: redirect URI is:
128: 
129: ```
130: http://localhost:8787/gatekeeper/cloudflare/oauth
131: ```
132: 
133: Register **exactly** this (replace the host with your `PUBLIC_BASE_URL` when not running locally) as
134: an allowed/pre-registered redirect URL on the Cloudflare OAuth client. If it isn't registered you'll
135: get an `invalid_request` error: _"the 'redirect_uri' parameter does not match any of the OAuth 2.0
136: Client's pre-registered redirect urls."_
137: 
138: ### Step 2: Configure Your Local Environment
139: 
140: Create a `.env` file in this package's directory (`packages/gatekeeper-cloudflare/.env`):
141: 
142: ```bash
143: CLIENT_ID=your-client-id-here
144: CLIENT_SECRET=your-client-secret-here
145: ```
146: 
147: In local dev, `run-dev-server.ts` will also seed these from `CLOUDFLARE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` /
148: `CLOUDFLARE_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET` if you'd rather set them in the root `.dev.vars`. A per-package
149: `.env` takes precedence and keeps the credential with the gatekeeper that uses it.
150: 
151: > **Note**: The `.env` file is gitignored and should never be committed.
152: 
153: ### Step 3: (Optional) Enable Cloudflare sign-in / billing
154: 
155: To offer "Continue with Cloudflare" on the login page, add `cloudflare` to the deployment's
156: `AUTH_GATEKEEPERS` allowlist (e.g. in the root `.dev.vars`):
157: 
158: ```
159: AUTH_GATEKEEPERS=cloudflare,google,github
160: ```
161: 
162: The order controls the order of the login buttons. For the AI Gateway billing / top-up flow, also
163: set `ENABLE_CLOUDFLARE_LIMITS=true` (see [AI Gateway billing](../../docs/ai-gateway-billing.md)); a
164: user enables billing by connecting Cloudflare, which requests the billing scopes
165: (`offline_access aig.read aig.run user-details.read account-settings.read`). Connecting all
166: Cloudflare gadget resources also requests `workers-observability.read`.
167: 
168: ### Step 4: Verify Setup
169: 
170: 1. Start the application in dev mode (see the root README.md).
171: 2. On the login page, click **Continue with Cloudflare**.
172: 3. A pop-up opens to the Cloudflare authorization page; approve it.
173: 4. The pop-up closes and you're signed in, identified by your Cloudflare account email.
174: 5. To use AI Gateway credits, open **Usage & billing** in settings and **Connect Cloudflare** (this
175:    requests billing scopes only).
176: 
177: ## Troubleshooting
178: 
179: ### "redirect_uri ... does not match any of the ... pre-registered redirect urls"
180: 
181: The redirect URI isn't registered on the OAuth client. Register exactly
182: `http://localhost:8787/gatekeeper/cloudflare/oauth` (or your `PUBLIC_BASE_URL` equivalent) — no
183: trailing slash, `http` not `https` for localhost.
184: 
185: ### "Not configured" page during authorization
186: 
187: `CLIENT_ID` / `CLIENT_SECRET` are missing. Ensure they're set (per-package `.env` or seeded from the
188: root `.dev.vars`), then restart the dev server.

(End of file - total 188 lines)
</content>

  Gateway.

  aggregate metrics, and traces either across an account or restricted to one Worker. Every result

Confirmed both ways — `telemetry/keys` on a live account reports `event`/`component`/`level` and no

But a provider error message can quote that same value straight back, so logging the message would

at all, so the error records separately whether the message is *its* or *ours*, and only ours is
logged. A provider failure carrying no codes is therefore logged as a bare status, which is the

The gatekeeper's OAuth redirect URI is:

```
${BASE_URL}/oauth
```

http://localhost:8787/gatekeeper/cloudflare/oauth

get an `invalid_request` error: _"the 'redirect_uri' parameter does not match any of the OAuth 2.0
Client's pre-registered redirect urls."_

### Step 2: Configure Your Local Environment

Create a `.env` file in this package's directory (`packages/gatekeeper-cloudflare/.env`):

```bash
CLIENT_ID=your-client-id-here
CLIENT_SECRET=your-client-secret-here
```

In local dev, `run-dev-server.ts` will also seed these from `CLOUDFLARE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` /
`CLOUDFLARE_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET` if you'd rather set them in the root `.dev.vars`. A per-package
`.env` takes precedence and keeps the credential with the gatekeeper that uses it.

> **Note**: The `.env` file is gitignored and should never be committed.

To offer "Continue with Cloudflare" on the login page, add `cloudflare` to the deployment's
`AUTH_GATEKEEPERS` allowlist (e.g. in the root `.dev.vars`):

```
AUTH_GATEKEEPERS=cloudflare,google,github
```

set `ENABLE_CLOUDFLARE_LIMITS=true` (see [AI Gateway billing](../../docs/ai-gateway-billing.md)); a
user enables billing by connecting Cloudflare, which requests the billing scopes
(`offline_access aig.read aig.run user-details.read account-settings.read`). Connecting all
Cloudflare gadget resources also requests `workers-observability.read`.

### Step 4: Verify Setup

1. Start the application in dev mode (see the root README.md).
2. On the login page, click **Continue with Cloudflare**.
3. A pop-up opens to the Cloudflare authorization page; approve it.
4. The pop-up closes and you're signed in, identified by your Cloudflare account email.
5. To use AI Gateway credits, open **Usage & billing** in settings and **Connect Cloudflare** (this
   requests billing scopes only).

### "redirect_uri ... does not match any of the ... pre-registered redirect urls"

The redirect URI isn't registered on the OAuth client. Register exactly
`http://localhost:8787/gatekeeper/cloudflare/oauth` (or your `PUBLIC_BASE_URL` equivalent) — no

change which upstream servers the session can reach, so granting one would let a Gadget widen its
own authority. This is a capability-boundary rule, not a policy preference, and is not configurable.

## Approvals and sharing

Identical to [`gatekeeper-mcp`](../gatekeeper-mcp/README.md#approvals-and-sharing), except for the
trust tier. A portal is an aggregator: `destructiveHint` and `idempotentHint` are written by
whichever upstream server it fronts, servers the administrator who chose the portal never reviewed,
and any one of them could self-declare both and get writes that skip the approval prompt. So the
tier is `byo` unless a deployment sets `MCP_PORTAL_TRUST_ANNOTATIONS=true`. That flag is the
"trusted server" assertion MCP's guidance asks for, and it has to be about the upstreams themselves,
not just the portal in front of them.

`addObserver` refuses everyone, as it does for user-supplied endpoints. Reaching the portal is not
the same as being allowed to see a particular tool result, and the Gadget runs on the owner's
credentials regardless. A sharper check is available here than for a bare endpoint —
`portal_list_servers` is per-user and Access-filtered, so it could confirm a collaborator may reach
the same server — but that is still server-granular, not record-granular. See
[`sharing-policy.ts`](../mcp-shared/src/sharing-policy.ts).

## Notes and current limitations

The limitations in
[`gatekeeper-mcp`](../gatekeeper-mcp/README.md#notes-and-current-limitations) apply here too: no
simulation, no revert, no hooks, no scoping below tool names, and `tools/*` only. SSRF is enforced
the same way, by `global_fetch_strictly_public` rather than by hostname patterns. In addition:

- **One portal per deployment.** `MCP_PORTAL_URL` is a single value; a second portal needs a
  second Worker.
- **Server ids come from tool-name prefixes.** An aggregator that flattens tools without prefixing
  them exposes no upstream seam, so this connector finds no server to scope a grant to and the form
  stays unsubmittable. It is not granted as a whole endpoint — that grant does not exist here. Use
  the **MCP** connector (`gatekeeper-mcp`) for such an endpoint, where endpoint-wide breadth is an
  explicit, reviewable choice.

## Layout

| File | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `src/portal.ts` | Vendor, account DO, user, gatekeeper facet, session, configurator RPC |
| `src/config.ts` | Reading and validating the deployment's portal configuration |
| `src/configurator/` | The grant UI (compiled into `src/generated/`) |

Everything else comes from [`@gadgets/mcp-shared`](../mcp-shared/README.md).

## Build & test

```
pnpm exec vp run -F @gadgets/mcp-portal-gatekeeper build   # build:configurator + tsc
pnpm --filter @gadgets/mcp-portal-gatekeeper test:run    # vitest
```

The Worker is run via the root `pnpm dev-server`, not directly.

# MCP shared

The protocol client, policy decisions, and stateful machinery common to the two MCP-speaking
gatekeepers. Not a Worker: a library both of them import.

| Package | Endpoint comes from | Grant is scoped to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`gatekeeper-mcp`](../gatekeeper-mcp/README.md) | a user pastes a URL | the whole server, or named tools |
| [`gatekeeper-mcp-portal`](../gatekeeper-mcp-portal/README.md) | a deployment var, `MCP_PORTAL_URL` | one upstream server behind the portal, or named tools |

security bug: tool classification, the scope grammar, the OAuth lifecycle, the approval-queue
wiring. A Worker's own vendor entrypoint, Durable Object classes and migrations, `Env`, connect
form, and configurator UI stay in the connector. Where a connector must vary shared behaviour it
does so through a named hook (`staticToken`, `mintAccount`), not a private copy.

## Modules

| Module | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `client` | Bounded Streamable HTTP transport (`initialize`, `tools/list`, `tools/call`) using official MCP wire types |
| `oauth` | Small adapter around the official MCP client's OAuth errors and token revocation gap |
| `tools` | The trust boundary: read/action classification, auto-approval eligibility, approval prompts, catalog fingerprinting |
| `schema-to-ts` | JSON Schema to TypeScript, strict `callTool` overloads plus progressive discovery |
| `session-methods` | Installs those methods at runtime, so the generated types are not a fiction |
| `tool-search` | The one query matcher every catalog search uses, so a query cannot mean two things |
| `portal` | Gateway detection, tool-name to upstream-server mapping, server listing |
| `scope` | The resource-URL scope grammar, and the check every call passes through |
| `endpoint` | Validation and host blocklist for a user-supplied endpoint |
| `fetch` | Every outbound request; redirects are followed by hand and each hop re-checked, including SDK OAuth fetches |
| `account` | Durable Object base and persisted SDK OAuth state: connect, refresh, revocation |
| `facet` | Common session, catalog, action, and sharing behavior for connector-owned Durable Object facets |
| `catalog` | One binding's tool list: fetched, cached, scoped to the grant, classified; plus the cache for tools hydrated past that list |
| `connection` | `withClient` — transport sessions, retries, credential-expiry reporting |
| `action-store` | Staged to applied/rejected/failed, with a bound on what is retained and a claim so one approval is never sent twice |
| `session` | The Gadget-facing capability, and the one path every tool call takes |
| `sharing-policy` | The owner-only sharing rule |
| `html` | The connect-flow pages, so both connectors look like one product |
| `http` | Base-path, OAuth callback, and connect-link routing shared by both Workers |
| `log` | The field vocabulary both connectors log against |
| `user` | The common account description, revocation, and reconnect lifecycle |
| `util` | Hex encoding, host extraction, binding-name slugs; no policy |
| `types.d.ts` | Base types prepended to every generated per-server `.d.ts` |

Nothing outside `tools.ts` reads a tool's `annotations`.

## Trust tiers

A tier governs how far a server's own claims about its tools are believed. MCP's own guidance is
that a client must treat tool annotations as untrusted unless they come from a trusted server, and
the tier is where this deployment records which servers those are. It is named by provenance, is
deployment configuration rather than account state, and is read at each point of use so withdrawing
it takes effect at once.

- **`byo`** — a user typed the URL in. `readOnlyHint` classifies reads; nothing the server says can
  auto-apply a write.
- **`vetted`** — a deployment has asserted this endpoint's annotations can be relied on, so
  `destructiveHint: false` plus `idempotentHint: true` may drive auto-approval. Configuring an
  endpoint is not by itself enough to earn this: a portal aggregates upstream servers whose
  annotations the administrator never saw, which is why `gatekeeper-mcp-portal` defaults to `byo`
  and requires `MCP_PORTAL_TRUST_ANNOTATIONS=true`.

with no approval, where an unlabelled one would have been queued. It is accepted because prompting
on every read makes the connector unusable for its main purpose, and because the owner chose to
connect the server. Auto-applying a write is not accepted on those terms.

Annotations are optional in MCP and most servers publish none. Every hint is compared with
`=== true` or `=== false`, so an unannotated tool is an action, needs approval, and can never
auto-apply, on either tier. That matches the spec's own defaults (`readOnlyHint: false`,
`destructiveHint: true`, `idempotentHint: false`).

Neither tier can be shared. A Gadget bound to any MCP endpoint is owner-only, for reasons unrelated
to provenance — see [`sharing-policy.ts`](src/sharing-policy.ts).

What an account records instead of a tier is `provenance`, `"user"` or `"deployment"`, settled when
it connects. Provenance decides whether a server may rename itself over an administrator's chosen
label in an approval prompt, which is a question that should not move when an annotation setting
does.

## Applying an approved call

The guarantee is *at most once*, not exactly once. MCP has no idempotency key that would make a
repeated call harmless and no inverse operation that would undo one, so where the two conflict the
store prefers losing a result over repeating a write.

An approval is claimed in storage before the call is sent, which is what stops two concurrent
`applyAction` calls from both reaching the server. Once the call returns, the record is settled in
its own small write *before* the result is attached, so nothing about handling a server-controlled
payload — normalizing it, encoding it, or finding it too large for the Durable Object to store — can
lose the fact that the write already happened.

Failures are split by what the server is known to have done, because that is not something the
caller can work out afterwards. Only a `401` or `403` proves the tool was refused before dispatch.
Generic HTTP and JSON-RPC errors, dropped connections, malformed replies, and oversized bodies all
leave the outcome unknown; those are closed as failed and **not** retryable, since the request may
already have been carried out. The classification (`callMayHaveTakenEffect`) fails safe: anything it
cannot positively identify as declined counts as possibly performed.

The same rule covers an activation dying between sending the call and recording the reply. The claim
is not released for another attempt: after `APPLY_CLAIM_TIMEOUT_MS` the action is closed the same
way, saying it may or may not have taken effect.

So the cost of a network blip is a call someone has to stage again, deliberately. That is the trade
this module makes everywhere: an approval is never spent twice without a person saying so.

Fixed rather than configurable.

| Limit | Value | Where | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Described or individually granted tools per server | 200 | `tools.ts` | Bounds the picker and generated `.d.ts`; a server-wide grant can discover additional tools later |
| Catalog size | 96 KiB UTF-8 | `client.ts` | Leaves room below Durable Object's 128 KiB per-value limit for the cache wrapper and serialization overhead |
| Filtered discovery scan | 5,000 tools / 4 MiB | `client.ts` | Bounds work spent skipping unrelated tools while searching a large endpoint |
| Search query / results | 200 chars / 20 tools | `tool-search.ts` | Bounds agent-supplied matching work and the summaries returned to it |
| Hydrated definitions per facet | 200 tools / 1 MiB | `catalog.ts` | Bounds definitions fetched individually beyond the described catalog |
| Tool description | 4 KB | `client.ts` | As above, per tool, before it reaches storage |
| Tool input schema | 20 KB | `client.ts` | Dropped rather than clipped; half a schema is not a schema |
| `tools/list` pages | 50 | `client.ts` | Stops a cursor that never ends; exhaustion truncates catalogs and fails exact/search discovery as a scan limit |
| Response body | 1 MiB | `fetch.ts` | Every response is buffered whole before it can be parsed, and a `tools/call` result is otherwise unbounded |
| Bounded outbound operation | 30 seconds | `fetch.ts` | OAuth and discovery callers opt into one deadline covering redirects, pagination, body streaming, and session retry |
| Retained result | 128 KB | `action-store.ts` | Held until the Gadget collects it; oversized ones are replaced by a note |
| Retained actions | 100 | `action-store.ts` | Records are for collecting a result, not an audit log |
| Actions awaiting a decision | 50 | `action-store.ts` | These cannot be pruned, so uncapped they are an unbounded write |
| Tool description in a prompt | 600 chars | `tools.ts` | Server-controlled text in a security decision |
| Tool arguments in a prompt | 4000 chars | `tools.ts` | Agent-controlled text in the same decision |
| Server name | 60 chars | `account.ts` | As above; also stripped of Markdown |
| Redirect hops | 3 | `fetch.ts` | Each one re-checked; more is a loop, not a deployment |
| Connect link | 10 min | `connect-nonce.ts` | Single-use, and consumed on success |
| Unfinished connect | 1 hour | `connect-nonce.ts` | After which a half-built account deletes itself |

pnpm --filter @gadgets/mcp-shared build   # tsc

# GitHub Gatekeeper Storage Schema

This gatekeeper uses Durable Object KV storage only. It does not use SQLite tables.

## Design choices

- Most resource and query caches use short-lived KV entries with stored ETags, while `since`-capable discussion streams use persistent prefix-plus-watermark sync caches.
- Simulation uses a read-time overlay for pending actions rather than mutating cached remote state in place.
- New issues and pull requests get provisional IDs like `~1`, `~2`, etc. Pending follow-up actions target those provisional IDs until the create action is applied.
- Applied review-comment aliases are recorded so later replies can resolve provisional comment IDs to GitHub comment IDs.
- Replies to provisional diff comments are intentionally not supported until the parent review is approved and GitHub assigns real comment IDs.

## UserAccount Durable Object

Keys:

- `callback` -> stored `GatekeeperConnectCallback` fetcher for the connected Workshop account.
- `nonce` -> `{ value: string, expiresAt: number, stage: "initiation" | "oauth" }`.
- `accessToken` -> GitHub OAuth access token string.
- `scopes` -> `string[]` of granted OAuth scopes.
- `expiredNotified` -> boolean guard so `credentialsExpired()` is only sent once per expired credential set.
- `reconnecting` -> boolean flag indicating an in-progress reconnect flow.

No per-user SQL tables are used.

## GitHubGatekeeperImpl Durable Object

### Counters

- `counter:action` -> next numeric suffix for action IDs (`a1`, `a2`, ...).

185:         ));
186:       break;
187:     case "reported-server":
188:       catalog = { tools: [], truncated: false };
189:       break;
190:     case "server-evidence":
191:       catalog = await withClient(env, account, endpoint,
192:         client => client.listMatchingToolIndex(
193:           1,
194:           tool => isPortalToolGrantable(tool.name, scope.serverId),
195:         ));
196:       break;

198:   return { scope, upstream: validateToolScopeAgainstCatalog(scope, catalog, servers) };

201: /**
202:  * The servers behind the portal, for the configurator's picker. Returns an empty list when the
203:  * endpoint is not a portal at all, but throws when it is one whose server list could not be read
204:  * completely: an incomplete picker would silently hide servers the user is entitled to grant.
205:  */
206: async function listAvailablePortalServers(
207:   env: Env,
208:   account: DurableObjectStub<McpAccount>,
209:   endpoint: string,
210: ): Promise<PortalServer[]> {
211:   const reported = await tryListPortalServers(env, account, endpoint);
212:   if (reported?.complete) return reported.servers;
213: 
214:   const index = await withClient(env, account, endpoint,
215:     client => client.listToolIndex(MAX_PORTAL_TOOL_INDEX));
216:   if (!looksLikePortal(
217:     index.tools, { truncated: index.truncated, cap: MAX_PORTAL_TOOL_INDEX })) return [];
218:   if (index.truncated) {
219:     throw new Error("Could not retrieve the portal's complete server list. Try again.");
220:   }
221:   return reconcilePortalServers(reported?.servers ?? [], index.tools);
222: }

224: // HTTP handler. There is no page asking which server to connect, since the endpoint is configured,
225: // so the only browser round trip is the portal's own authorization.
226: 
227: export default {
228:   async fetch(req: Request, env: Env, ctx: ExecutionContext): Promise<Response> {
229:     return handleMcpHttpRequest(req, {
230:       baseUrl: getBaseUrl(env),
231:       accountForId: id => ctx.exports.McpAccount.get(
232:         ctx.exports.McpAccount.idFromString(id)),
233:       log: logger,
234:       connect: async (request, account, initiationNonce) => {
235:         if (request.method !== "GET") return new Response("Method Not Allowed", { status: 405 });
236:         return continueConnect(account, initiationNonce, env);
237:       },
238:     });
239:   },
240: };

242: // Hands off to the account DO, which owns every credential. The target comes from configuration, so
243: // this is the same call for a first connect and a reconnect.
244: async function continueConnect(
245:   account: DurableObjectStub<McpAccount>,
246:   initiationNonce: string,
247:   env: Env,
248: ): Promise<Response> {
249:   const config = readPortalConfig(env);
250:   if (!config) {
251:     return htmlResponse(errorPageHtml(
252:       "No MCP server portal is configured",
253:       "Ask an administrator to set this deployment's MCP server portal URL."), 503);
254:   }
255: 
256:   let outcome: ConnectOutcome;
257:   try {
258:     outcome = await account.beginConnect(initiationNonce, portalServer(config));
259:   } catch (err) {
260:     logger.warn("connect failed", { event: "connect.failed", error: err });
261:     return htmlResponse(errorPageHtml(
262:       "Could not connect", err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err)), 502);
263:   }
264: 
265:   if (outcome.kind === "invalid") return htmlResponse(INVALID_LINK_HTML, 400);
266:   if (outcome.kind === "redirect") return Response.redirect(outcome.url, 302);
267:   return htmlResponse(SELF_CLOSING_HTML);

275:   async describe(): Promise<VendorDescription> {

278:       displayName: config?.name ?? "Cloudflare MCP Server Portals",
279:       url: "https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/ai-controls/mcp-portals/",
280:       logo: PORTAL_AVATAR,

282:       tagline: config

296:     const initiationNonce = generateNonce();
297:     await this.ctx.exports.McpAccount.get(accountId).setCallback(callback, initiationNonce);

301:   /**
302:    * The one resource this connector offers, or none when unconfigured. Returning nothing is how the
303:    * connector hides itself: the Workshop drops a vendor that advertises no resources.

312:     // generated per resource, from the chosen upstream server's own catalog; see

325:  * real addition: a portal may be fronted by one instead of using OAuth.

355:   extends McpGatekeeperUserBase<Env>

358:   #account(): DurableObjectStub<McpAccount> {

360:       this.ctx.exports.McpAccount.idFromString(this.ctx.props.accountObjectId));

363:   protected [mcpGatekeeperUserContext]() {

367:   /**
368:    * The portal as currently configured, not as it was when this account connected. Repointing the
369:    * deployment therefore surfaces as a reconnect, via `getGatekeeperClassFor` refusing the old
370:    * endpoint, rather than as a Gadget quietly talking to a portal nobody chose.
371:    */
372:   async getSupportedResources(): Promise<SupportedResource[]> {
373:     const config = readPortalConfig(this.env);
374:     return config ? [portalResource(config)] : [];
375:   }

377:   async getGatekeeperClassFor(url: string): Promise<{
378:     class: DurableObjectClass<Gatekeeper<unknown>>;
379:     resource: SupportedResource;
380:   }> {
381:     const config = readPortalConfig(this.env);
382:     if (!config) {
383:       throw new Error("This deployment has no MCP server portal configured.");
384:     }
385:     const server = await this.#account().getServer();
386:     const resource = portalResource(config);
387: 
388:     // The account connected to one portal and the deployment now names one; a repoint between the
389:     // two must surface as a reconnect. Otherwise this facet would be minted against the endpoint
390:     // frozen on the account while the deployment believes it configured a different one.
391:     if (!sameEndpoint(server.endpoint, config.endpoint)) {
392:       throw new Error(
393:         `This connection is for ${hostOf(server.endpoint)}, but this deployment's portal is now ` +
394:         `${hostOf(config.endpoint)}. Reconnect the account.`);
395:     }
396:     if (portalAuthRequiresReconnect(server.auth, config.auth)) {
397:       throw new Error("This deployment's portal authentication changed. Reconnect the account.");
398:     }
399: 
400:     // The account holds credentials for one portal, so a resource URL naming any other endpoint is
401:     // not this account's to grant. Compared in full rather than by origin: one host can front `/mcp`
402:     // and `/mcp-v2` as unrelated endpoints, and the facet always calls the endpoint recorded on the
403:     // account, so an origin-only test would honour a grant against a URL nobody connected to.
404:     const requested = new URL(url, server.endpoint);
405:     if (!sameEndpoint(requested.toString(), config.endpoint)) {
406:       throw new Error(
407:         `This connection is for ${config.endpoint}, not ` +
408:         `${endpointOfResourceUrl(requested)}.`);
409:     }
410:     if (!matchesResourceUrlPattern(resource.urlPattern, requested.toString())) {
411:       throw new Error(`"${url}" does not match this connection's resource type.`);
412:     }
413: 
414:     const account = this.#account();
415:     const { scope, upstream } = await validatePortalScope(
416:       this.env, account, server.endpoint, requested);
417: 
418:     const props: McpGatekeeperImplProps = {
419:       accountObjectId: this.ctx.props.accountObjectId,
420:       endpoint: server.endpoint,
421:       serverId: server.serverId,
422:       serverName: config.name,
423:       scopeServerName: upstream?.name ?? scope.serverId,
424:       scope,
425:     };
426:     return { class: this.ctx.exports.McpGatekeeperImpl({ props }), resource };
427:   }

429:   async startResourceConfigurator(_resourceUrlPattern: string): Promise<ResourceConfiguratorFrame> {
430:     return {
431:       iframeHtml: MCP_SERVER_CONFIGURATOR_HTML,

458: @validateRpc()

465:   constructor(env: Env, account: DurableObjectStub<McpAccount>) {

468:     this.#account = account;

471:   async getEndpoint(): Promise<string> {

475:   #server(): Promise<ConnectedServer> {
476:     return this.#serverPromise ??= this.#account.getServer();
477:   }

481:       const server = await this.#server();

486:   // Ask the portal for its server index without first loading every upstream tool. Empty for an
487:   // endpoint that does not implement the portal contract or currently fronts nothing; either case
488:   // leaves the form unsubmittable.
489:   async listServerOptions(): Promise<ConfiguratorUIOption[]> {
490:     return (await this.#portalServers())
491:       .filter(upstream => !isPortalServerHidden(this.#env, upstream.id))
492:       .map(upstream => ({
493:         value: upstream.id,
494:         title: upstream.name,
495:         // A server can be configured but switched off for this session, making a grant onto it valid
496:         // but presently empty, which the person choosing should see.
497:         meta: upstream.enabled ? undefined : "disabled in portal",

501:   // Tools the grant may cover within one portal upstream server. The survey is checked before the
502:   // detailed catalog is fetched, and `toolGrantOptions` decides what each source says.
503:   async listToolOptions(serverId: string): Promise<ConfiguratorUIOption[]> {
504:     if (!isValidToolName(serverId) || isPortalServerHidden(this.#env, serverId)) return [];
505:     if (!(await this.#portalServers()).some(server => server.id === serverId)) return [];
506:     const server = await this.#server();
507:     const tools = await withClient(this.#env, this.#account, server.endpoint,
508:       client => client.listMatchingToolSummaries(
509:         MAX_TOOLS_PER_SERVER,
510:         tool => isPortalToolGrantable(tool.name, serverId),
511:       ));

523: // Props identifying which server (and how much of it) a gatekeeper facet governs. The trust tier is
524: // absent: it is deployment configuration, read from `portalTrust(this.env)` at each point of use,
525: // since baking it into props would pin every binding to the setting on the day it was created.
526: type McpGatekeeperImplProps = {
527:   accountObjectId: string;
528:   endpoint: string;
529:   serverId: string;
530:   serverName: string;
531:   // Optional for facets minted before catalog-backed validation persisted the upstream display name.

537: export class McpGatekeeperImpl
538:   extends McpFacetBase<Env, McpGatekeeperImplProps, McpSessionImpl> {
539: 
540:   protected get log() {
541:     return logger.with({
542:       serverId: this.ctx.props.serverId,

553:   protected get trust(): ServerTrust {

557:   protected get sessionClass() {

561:   protected get observerName(): string {

565:   // How this binding's breadth reads to a human, for approval prompts and the bindings list.
566:   #scopeLabel(): string {

568:     return `${serverName} / ${scopeServerName ?? scope.serverId}`;
569:   }

571:   async describe(): Promise<ResourceDescription> {
572:     const tools = await this.tools();
573:     const reads = tools.filter(entry => entry.mode === "read").length;
574:     const { scope } = this.ctx.props;
575:     const label = this.#scopeLabel();

577:     const counts = `${reads} read-only, ${tools.length - reads} requiring approval`;
578:     const plural = tools.length === 1 ? "" : "s";
579:     const snippet = scope.tools
580:       ? `${scope.tools.length} named MCP tool${scope.tools.length === 1 ? "" : "s"} on ` +
581:         `${label} \u2014 ${counts}. Other tools are refused.`

583:         `${this.ctx.props.serverName}; ${tools.length} tool definition${plural} shown here ` +
584:         `(${counts}). Use listTools({ search }) for others. Other servers are refused.`;
585: 
586:     return {
587:       url: this.resourceUrl,
588:       title: scope.tools?.length === 1 ? `${label}: ${scope.tools[0]}` : label,
589:       snippet,
590:       suggestedBindingName: `MCP_${bindingNameFragment(this.#bindingId())}`,

595:   // Identifies this binding's shape for naming. Server-scoped bindings get their own suggested name
596:   // and session type, so two bindings onto different servers of one portal do not collide and the
597:   // agent's type for the GitHub half of a portal is named after GitHub.

600:   // server produce the same id. `sessionTypeName` is what separates them, from the scoped resource

<content>
1: # Scheduled Tasks
2: 
3: Scheduled Tasks is an ambient Gatekeeper that lets workspace code register persistent callbacks for
4: elapsed intervals, wall-clock recurrences, and one-time runs. Each account also gets a read-only
5: management app at `/gatekeepers/scheduler`.
6: 
7: ## User flow
8: 
9: 1. Ask the agent to create a scheduled task, or open **Scheduled** and choose a starter prompt.
10: 2. Confirm what the task should do, the workspace and resources it may use, its cadence, and its
11:    IANA timezone when it uses wall-clock time.
12: 3. The agent registers a persistent callback. Registration creates a disabled hook and returns its
13:    schedule ID; it does not start the schedule.
14: 4. Enable the hook in the Workshop's Connections UI.
15: 5. Use **Scheduled** to search and inspect schedules across the account. Select a schedule row to
16:    open its workspace.
17: 
18: The Scheduler app is intentionally read-only. Enabling and disabling remain in Connections; the app
19: does not provide editing, pausing, deletion, run history, or a second hook toggle.
20: 
21: ## Agent API
22: 
23: The ambient binding exposes `ScheduleSession`. The exact agent-facing contract and examples live in
24: [`src/types.d.ts`](src/types.d.ts).
25: 
26: ```ts
27: const callback = await ctx.restore({ type: "dailyBrief" });
28: 
29: const scheduleId = await SCHEDULER.calendarAt(
30:   {
31:     timeZone: "America/Chicago",
32:     freq: "weekly",
33:     byDay: ["MO", "TU", "WE", "TH", "FR"],
34:     hour: 8,
35:     minute: 0,
36:   },
37:   callback,
38:   {
39:     title: "Daily brief",
40:     description: "Prepare the morning calendar and inbox brief.",
41:     occurrences: { count: 10 },
42:   },
43: );
44: ```
45: 
46: Use the three registration methods according to the user's intent:
47: 
48: - `every(everyMs, callback, options)` uses elapsed UTC time. The minimum interval is 60 seconds.
49: - `calendarAt(rule, callback, options)` follows local wall-clock time and requires an explicit IANA
50:   timezone. It supports hourly, daily, and weekly rules.
51: - `runAt(when, callback, options)` runs once at an absolute epoch-millisecond timestamp or an
52:   explicit timezone-aware wall-clock time.
53: 
54: Recurring `every()` and `calendarAt()` calls may stop after a finite bound. Give one or the other,
55: never both; `runAt()` accepts neither.
56: 
57: - `occurrences: { count: 10 }` allows ten logical scheduled occurrences.
58: - `occurrences: { until: { timeZone, year, month, day, hour, minute } }` allows occurrences through
59:   that instant, inclusively. An absolute epoch-millisecond `until` is also accepted. Registration
60:   rejects a cutoff that precedes the schedule's first occurrence.
61: 
62: The count bounds *due slots*, not successful runs. A slot consumes one count as soon as it becomes
63: due and takes a `runId`, even if admission or callback delivery then fails; admission failures skip
64: the slot without retrying it. Retries reuse the same `runId` and do not consume another count.
65: Missed occurrences remain skipped and do not count.
66: 
67: A bound is checked against live state, so a schedule that reaches it reports `completed`. A schedule
68: whose cutoff already passed by the time its hook is enabled reports `expired` instead: it never got
69: a slot. A schedule whose callback exhausts its eight attempts reports `dead` and stops there,
70: whether or not the bound was reached — a `count: 10` schedule that dies on its third occurrence
71: never reaches the fourth. Disabling a hook drops its driver state, so re-enabling the same schedule
72: restarts the count — treat `count` as a bound per enablement, not a lifetime guarantee.
73: 
74: `list()` returns active and terminal schedules for enabled hooks in the current workspace only. It
75: does not expose schedules from other workspaces in the account.
76: 
77: ## Persistent callbacks and retries
78: 
79: Callbacks implement `ScheduledTaskHook.onSchedule()` and must be made persistent with
80: `ctx.restore()` before registration. Each firing contains:
81: 
82: - `scheduleId`, the stable registration ID;
83: - `runId`, stable across retries of one logical occurrence;
84: - `scheduledTime`, the planned Unix epoch time;
85: - `actualTime`, the current delivery-attempt time; and
86: - `timeZone`, the schedule's display timezone (`UTC` for elapsed intervals and numeric one-shots).
87: 
88: Callback delivery is best-effort within a bounded retry window and may occur more than once. Callback
89: code should use `runId` as an idempotency key. Authorization or callback failures retry up to eight
90: total attempts with exponential delays beginning at one minute and capped at one hour. Exhausted
91: schedules enter the **Needs attention** state.
92: 
93: The Workshop admission check runs before every attempt. If the hook, gatekeeper, or account is no
94: longer allowed, the occurrence is skipped without consuming a callback attempt. Recurring schedules
95: advance to their next future occurrence; a due one-shot expires.
96: 
97: ## Cadence behavior
98: 
99: - Recurrences preserve the phase established at registration.
100: - Missed occurrences are skipped, not replayed or caught up.
101: - Fixed intervals measure elapsed time and therefore shift relative to local clocks across DST.
102: - Calendar schedules retain their requested local wall-clock cadence across DST.
103: - A nonexistent spring-forward time moves forward by the transition gap.
104: - An ambiguous fall-back time uses the earlier instant and fires once.
105: - Date-less wall-clock one-shots resolve to the next future occurrence of that local time.
106: 
107: Always ask the user for the timezone of a wall-clock schedule. Do not infer it from locale or silently
108: choose UTC.
109: 
110: ## Lifecycle
111: 
112: Registration only binds a disabled Workshop hook; it writes no schedule row. Enabling records the
113: target workspace ID and optional gadget ID, then creates the account-driver row and arms its alarm.
114: Disabling removes the row and its stored capabilities. Re-enabling creates fresh active state,
115: preserves the original recurrence phase, and does not replay missed work. A repeated enable while
116: the row still exists instead preserves its current schedule state and refreshes its activation details.
117: 
118: Successful one-shots become **Finished**. Past or rejected one-shots become expired. Terminal rows
119: remain visible and consume enabled-schedule quota until their hook is disabled in Connections.
120: Creating a workspace from a blueprint does not copy schedules or capabilities: the new workspace must
121: register its callback and receive fresh enablement.
122: 
123: Disconnecting the Scheduler account revokes its driver, deletes schedule state, and leaves a permanent
124: tombstone so retained stale controllers cannot recreate the account.
125: 
126: ## Management app
127: 
128: The account advertises its UI through the generic `AccountDescription.providesUi` mechanism, the same
129: mechanism used by other Gatekeeper management apps. The Workshop discovers it dynamically and hosts
130: the single-file app in an opaque-origin, network-isolated `srcDoc` frame.
131: 
132: The app can only call its account-scoped, read-only `list()` capability plus bounded host methods for
133: theme updates, workspace-title resolution, navigation, and starter prompts. Pages contain at most 100
134: schedules. Search is case-insensitive over title and description and is limited to 200 characters.
135: Cursors are opaque, bounded, and tied to the normalized search and status filters.
136: 
137: The **All**, **Active**, **Needs attention**, and **Finished** tabs map to the projected
138: `active`, `dead`, and `completed`/`expired` statuses. Target metadata is presentation data only;
139: opening its validated internal route grants no new authority. Create and starter actions place fixed
140: editable text in the Home composer and never submit it automatically.
141: 
142: ## Architecture and security
143: 
144: Each Scheduler account owns one SQLite-backed `ScheduleDriver` Durable Object and one alarm for all of
145: its workspaces. Workspace sessions inherit their opaque scope from the containing Overseer facet;
146: callers cannot supply an account or workspace ID. Plain schedule metadata and reconstructable RPC
147: capabilities are stored under separate keys and changed transactionally.
148: 
149: The alarm persists state before crossing an RPC boundary. It processes at most 20 due schedules per
150: pass with four concurrent deliveries, then arms an immediate continuation when a backlog remains.
151: Stable `runId` fencing prevents late completion or retry continuations from mutating a disabled,
152: re-enabled, or revoked schedule.
153: 
154: One account-wide driver keeps management and revocation simple, but it is also a shared failure domain:
155: a user callback that never settles can delay other schedules in that account until the runtime aborts
156: the alarm. Bounded batches limit ordinary load; they do not eliminate that tradeoff.
157: 
158: The Scheduler is capability-authorized. It does not receive Workshop user identity, assert its own
159: ambient policy, expose external network authority, or implement actions. The Workshop's existing hook
160: admission and observation authorization remain the security boundaries.
161: 
162: ## Limits
163: 
164: - 500 enabled or terminal schedule rows per account.
165: - 100 enabled or terminal schedule rows per workspace.
166: - 100 rows per management page.
167: - 20 due schedules per alarm pass and four concurrent deliveries.
168: - Eight callback attempts per logical occurrence.
169: - Schedule titles: 200 characters; descriptions: 2,000 characters.
170: 
171: These are fixed policy limits rather than deployment settings.
172: 
173: ## Development
174: 
175: Install and build from the repository root:
176: 
177: ```sh
178: pnpm install
179: pnpm --filter @gadgets/gatekeeper-scheduler test:run
180: pnpm --filter @gadgets/gatekeeper-scheduler build
181: pnpm run dev-server
182: pnpm run dev-client
183: ```
184: 
185: The development server discovers `gatekeeper-*` packages, builds `app/` into the generated single-file
186: asset, and creates the local `GATEKEEPER_SCHEDULER` service binding. Do not edit generated local
187: Wrangler configuration.
188: 
189: Worker code gets its runtime and `Cloudflare.Env` types from generated
190: [`worker-configuration.d.ts`](worker-configuration.d.ts), referenced by `tsconfig.json`. Regenerate it
191: with Wrangler after changing Worker configuration; do not hand-maintain a parallel `Env` interface.
192: The browser app uses the separate DOM-only `tsconfig.app.json` and imports only environment-neutral
193: management DTOs.
194: 
195: ## Deployment
196: 
197: Before exposing Scheduler:
198: 
199: 1. Deploy the Workshop hook target-metadata contract and the `startHook()` admission backstop.
200: 2. Deploy this Worker so its `ScheduleDriver` and `SchedulerGatekeeper` SQLite migration exists.
201: 3. Add `GATEKEEPER_SCHEDULER` to the deployment's Workshop service bindings.
202: 
203: Scheduler declares only that it can auto-provision an account. Workshop provisioning policy defaults
204: the `scheduler` vendor to **optional**; an administrator can explicitly choose disabled, optional, or
205: enabled. Production service bindings are site-specific and are not generated by this package.
206: 
207: The `allow_irrevocable_stub_storage` compatibility flag is required while stored callback capabilities
208: exist and must not be removed from an existing deployment.

display.text:
# Scheduled Tasks

Scheduled Tasks is an ambient Gatekeeper that lets workspace code register persistent callbacks for
elapsed intervals, wall-clock recurrences, and one-time runs. Each account also gets a read-only
management app at `/gatekeepers/scheduler`.

## User flow

1. Ask the agent to create a scheduled task, or open **Scheduled** and choose a starter prompt.
2. Confirm what the task should do, the workspace and resources it may use, its cadence, and its
   IANA timezone when it uses wall-clock time.
3. The agent registers a persistent callback. Registration creates a disabled hook and returns its
   schedule ID; it does not start the schedule.
4. Enable the hook in the Workshop's Connections UI.
5. Use **Scheduled** to search and inspect schedules across the account. Select a schedule row to
   open its workspace.

The Scheduler app is intentionally read-only. Enabling and disabling remain in Connections; the app
does not provide editing, pausing, deletion, run history, or a second hook toggle.

## Agent API

The ambient binding exposes `ScheduleSession`. The exact agent-facing contract and examples live in
[`src/types.d.ts`](src/types.d.ts).

```ts
const callback = await ctx.restore({ type: "dailyBrief" });

const scheduleId = await SCHEDULER.calendarAt(
  {
    timeZone: "America/Chicago",
    freq: "weekly",
    byDay: ["MO", "TU", "WE", "TH", "FR"],
    hour: 8,
    minute: 0,
  },
  callback,
  {
    title: "Daily brief",
    description: "Prepare the morning calendar and inbox brief.",
    occurrences: { count: 10 },
  },
);
```

Use the three registration methods according to the user's intent:

- `every(everyMs, callback, options)` uses elapsed UTC time. The minimum interval is 60 seconds.
- `calendarAt(rule, callback, options)` follows local wall-clock time and requires an explicit IANA
  timezone. It supports hourly, daily, and weekly rules.
- `runAt(when, callback, options)` runs once at an absolute epoch-millisecond timestamp or an
  explicit timezone-aware wall-clock time.

Recurring `every()` and `calendarAt()` calls may stop after a finite bound. Give one or the other,
never both; `runAt()` accepts neither.

- `occurrences: { count: 10 }` allows ten logical scheduled occurrences.
- `occurrences: { until: { timeZone, year, month, day, hour, minute } }` allows occurrences through
  that instant, inclusively. An absolute epoch-millisecond `until` is also accepted. Registration
  rejects a cutoff that precedes the schedule's first occurrence.

The count bounds *due slots*, not successful runs. A slot consumes one count as soon as it becomes
due and takes a `runId`, even if admission or callback delivery then fails; admission failures skip
the slot without retrying it. Retries reuse the same `runId` and do not consume another count.
Missed occurrences remain skipped and do not count.

A bound is checked against live state, so a schedule that reaches it reports `completed`. A schedule
whose cutoff already passed by the time its hook is enabled reports `expired` instead: it never got
a slot. A schedule whose callback exhausts its eight attempts reports `dead` and stops there,
whether or not the bound was reached — a `count: 10` schedule that dies on its third occurrence
never reaches the fourth. Disabling a hook drops its driver state, so re-enabling the same schedule
restarts the count — treat `count` as a bound per enablement, not a lifetime guarantee.

`list()` returns active and terminal schedules for enabled hooks in the current workspace only. It
does not expose schedules from other workspaces in the account.

## Persistent callbacks and retries

Callbacks implement `ScheduledTaskHook.onSchedule()` and must be made persistent with
`ctx.restore()` before registration. Each firing contains:

- `scheduleId`, the stable registration ID;
- `runId`, stable across retries of one logical occurrence;
- `scheduledTime`, the planned Unix epoch time;
- `actualTime`, the current delivery-attempt time; and
- `timeZone`, the schedule's display timezone (`UTC` for elapsed intervals and numeric one-shots).

Callback delivery is best-effort within a bounded retry window and may occur more than once. Callback
code should use `runId` as an idempotency key. Authorization or callback failures retry up to eight
total attempts with exponential delays beginning at one minute and capped at one hour. Exhausted
schedules enter the **Needs attention** state.

The Workshop admission check runs before every attempt. If the hook, gatekeeper, or account is no
longer allowed, the occurrence is skipped without consuming a callback attempt. Recurring schedules
advance to their next future occurrence; a due one-shot expires.

## Cadence behavior

- Recurrences preserve the phase established at registration.
- Missed occurrences are skipped, not replayed or caught up.
- Fixed intervals measure elapsed time and therefore shift relative to local clocks across DST.
- Calendar schedules retain their requested local wall-clock cadence across DST.
- A nonexistent spring-forward time moves forward by the transition gap.
- An ambiguous fall-back time uses the earlier instant and fires once.
- Date-less wall-clock one-shots resolve to the next future occurrence of that local time.

Always ask the user for the timezone of a wall-clock schedule. Do not infer it from locale or silently
choose UTC.

## Lifecycle

Registration only binds a disabled Workshop hook; it writes no schedule row. Enabling records the
target workspace ID and optional gadget ID, then creates the account-driver row and arms its alarm.
Disabling removes the row and its stored capabilities. Re-enabling creates fresh active state,
preserves the original recurrence phase, and does not replay missed work. A repeated enable while
the row still exists instead preserves its current schedule state and refreshes its activation details.

Successful one-shots become **Finished**. Past or rejected one-shots become expired. Terminal rows
remain visible and consume enabled-schedule quota until their hook is disabled in Connections.
Creating a workspace from a blueprint does not copy schedules or capabilities: the new workspace must
register its callback and receive fresh enablement.

Disconnecting the Scheduler account revokes its driver, deletes schedule state, and leaves a permanent
tombstone so retained stale controllers cannot recreate the account.

## Management app

The account advertises its UI through the generic `AccountDescription.providesUi` mechanism, the same
mechanism used by other Gatekeeper management apps. The Workshop discovers it dynamically and hosts
the single-file app in an opaque-origin, network-isolated `srcDoc` frame.

The app can only call its account-scoped, read-only `list()` capability plus bounded host methods for
theme updates, workspace-title resolution, navigation, and starter prompts. Pages contain at most 100
schedules. Search is case-insensitive over title and description and is limited to 200 characters.
Cursors are opaque, bounded, and tied to the normalized search and status filters.

The **All**, **Active**, **Needs attention**, and **Finished** tabs map to the projected
`active`, `dead`, and `completed`/`expired` statuses. Target metadata is presentation data only;
opening its validated internal route grants no new authority. Create and starter actions place fixed
editable text in the Home composer and never submit it automatically.

## Architecture and security

Each Scheduler account owns one SQLite-backed `ScheduleDriver` Durable Object and one alarm for all of
its workspaces. Workspace sessions inherit their opaque scope from the containing Overseer facet;
callers cannot supply an account or workspace ID. Plain schedule metadata and reconstructable RPC
capabilities are stored under separate keys and changed transactionally.

The alarm persists state before crossing an RPC boundary. It processes at most 20 due schedules per
pass with four concurrent deliveries, then arms an immediate continuation when a backlog remains.
Stable `runId` fencing prevents late completion or retry continuations from mutating a disabled,
re-enabled, or revoked schedule.

One account-wide driver keeps management and revocation simple, but it is also a shared failure domain:
a user callback that never settles can delay other schedules in that account until the runtime aborts
the alarm. Bounded batches limit ordinary load; they do not eliminate that tradeoff.

The Scheduler is capability-authorized. It does not receive Workshop user identity, assert its own
ambient policy, expose external network authority, or implement actions. The Workshop's existing hook
admission and observation authorization remain the security boundaries.

## Limits

- 500 enabled or terminal schedule rows per account.
- 100 enabled or terminal schedule rows per workspace.
- 100 rows per management page.
- 20 due schedules per alarm pass and four concurrent deliveries.
- Eight callback attempts per logical occurrence.
- Schedule titles: 200 characters; descriptions: 2,000 characters.

These are fixed policy limits rather than deployment settings.

## Development

Install and build from the repository root:

```sh
pnpm install
pnpm --filter @gadgets/gatekeeper-scheduler test:run
pnpm --filter @gadgets/gatekeeper-scheduler build
pnpm run dev-server
pnpm run dev-client
```

The development server discovers `gatekeeper-*` packages, builds `app/` into the generated single-file
asset, and creates the local `GATEKEEPER_SCHEDULER` service binding. Do not edit generated local
Wrangler configuration.

Worker code gets its runtime and `Cloudflare.Env` types from generated
[`worker-configuration.d.ts`](worker-configuration.d.ts), referenced by `tsconfig.json`. Regenerate it
with Wrangler after changing Worker configuration; do not hand-maintain a parallel `Env` interface.
The browser app uses the separate DOM-only `tsconfig.app.json` and imports only environment-neutral
management DTOs.

## Deployment

Before exposing Scheduler:

1. Deploy the Workshop hook target-metadata contract and the `startHook()` admission backstop.
2. Deploy this Worker so its `ScheduleDriver` and `SchedulerGatekeeper` SQLite migration exists.
3. Add `GATEKEEPER_SCHEDULER` to the deployment's Workshop service bindings.

Scheduler declares only that it can auto-provision an account. Workshop provisioning policy defaults
the `scheduler` vendor to **optional**; an administrator can explicitly choose disabled, optional, or
enabled. Production service bindings are site-specific and are not generated by this package.

The `allow_irrevocable_stub_storage` compatibility flag is required while stored callback capabilities
exist and must not be removed from an existing deployment.

## Troubleshooting

- **Scheduled is missing from navigation:** confirm the Scheduler binding exists, the vendor is enabled
  or optional with a connected account, and account discovery returns `providesUi`.
- **A new schedule is not listed or running:** registration starts disabled. Enable its hook in the
  workspace Connections UI.
- **A schedule says Needs attention:** callback authorization or execution exhausted its retry budget.
  Fix the callback or resource access, then disable and re-enable the hook.
- **A one-shot says Expired:** its firing time passed without admission or it was already past when
  enabled. Register a new future one-shot.
- **A recurrence appears an hour off:** use `calendarAt()` for local wall-clock intent and `every()` for
  elapsed time; verify the explicit IANA timezone.
- **A blueprint-created workspace has no schedules:** schedules are deliberately not copied. Register
  them again in the new workspace.

## Non-goals

V1 does not provide schedule editing, local pause/toggle/delete controls, recurring run history,
`lastRunAt`, account default timezones, actor attribution, blueprint schedule cloning, catch-up delivery,
or collaborator-owned schedule routing. Hook lifecycle remains in the Workshop Connections UI.

204: export function hasDriveResourceGrant(resourceUrlPatterns: readonly string[]): boolean {
205:   return resourceUrlPatterns.some(pattern => DRIVE_RESOURCE_PATTERNS.has(pattern));
206: }

208: /** Rejects any pattern that is not a known grantable resource. */
209: export function validateResourceUrlPatterns(resourceUrlPatterns: readonly string[]): void {
210:   let unknown = resourceUrlPatterns.filter(pattern => !KNOWN_RESOURCE_PATTERNS.has(pattern));
211:   if (unknown.length > 0) {
212:     throw new Error(`Unknown grantable resource URL pattern(s): ${unknown.join(", ")}`);

216: /** The OAuth scopes required by the explicit grantable resource `urlPattern`s. */
217: export function resourceUrlPatternsToOAuthScopes(resourceUrlPatterns: readonly string[]): string[] {
218:   validateResourceUrlPatterns(resourceUrlPatterns);

220:   let scopes = new Set<string>(IDENTITY_SCOPES);
221:   for (let entry of RESOURCE_SCOPES) {
222:     if (resourceUrlPatterns.includes(entry.resource.urlPattern)) {

237:     grantedOAuthScopes: readonly string[]): string[] {

240:   return RESOURCE_SCOPES
241:       .filter(entry => requested.has(entry.resource.urlPattern) &&
242:                        entry.scopes.every(scope => granted.has(scope)))
243:       .map(entry => entry.resource.urlPattern);

246: /** A resource URL resolved to the binding parameters its gatekeeper takes. */
247: export type ResourceTarget =
248:   | { kind: "gmail"; searchQuery?: string; labelName?: string }
249:   | { kind: "doc"; documentId: string }
250:   | { kind: "sheets"; spreadsheetId: string }
251:   | { kind: "calendar"; calendarId: string; availabilityMode: CalendarAvailabilityMode }
252:   | { kind: "bigquery"; projectId: string; datasetId?: string; tableId?: string }
253:   | { kind: "driveAccount" }
254:   | { kind: "sharedDrive"; driveId: string }
255:   | { kind: "driveFile"; fileId: string };

257: /** The grantable resource each {@link ResourceTarget} kind belongs to. */
258: export const RESOURCE_BY_KIND: Record<ResourceTarget["kind"], SupportedResource> = {
259:   gmail: GMAIL_RESOURCE,
260:   doc: GOOGLE_DOC_RESOURCE,
261:   sheets: GOOGLE_SHEETS_RESOURCE,
262:   calendar: GOOGLE_CALENDAR_RESOURCE,
263:   bigquery: BIGQUERY_RESOURCE,
264:   driveAccount: GOOGLE_DRIVE_RESOURCE,
265:   sharedDrive: GOOGLE_SHARED_DRIVE_RESOURCE,
266:   driveFile: GOOGLE_DRIVE_FILE_RESOURCE,
267: };
